title: Do Verifiers Reduce Security-Relevant Misconfigurations? A Preregistered Paired Evaluation of Verifier-in-the-Loop GVR for Intent-to-Configuration
abstract: We preregistered and executed a deterministic paired experiment to test whether embedding a reachability/policy verifier inside a generate–verify–repair (GVR) loop reduces security-increasing (forbidden-reachability) misconfigurations produced by an LLM-driven intent→configuration pipeline. Using Dockerized FRRouting-style emulation, two deterministic validators combined with a logical-OR scoring rule, and a matched sample of N = 300 intents (150 benign + 150 programmatic adversarial variants), we compared single-pass LLM generation (baseline) to an LLM+verifier GVR pipeline implemented under a frozen protocol (preregistration cnd-2026-netops-gvr-security-01-prereg-v1). The adapter used shared_initial_candidate semantics: one initial LLM candidate was generated per paired intent and the same candidate was replayed to both arms (baseline is therefore not an independent-generation condition). The run completed all planned episodes with model_calls_used = 300 (shared candidate). Confirmatory outcome: baseline_success = 300 and guarded_success = 300 (contingency n11 = 300, n10 = n01 = n00 = 0); validators never reported forbidden reachability and the repair step was never invoked. Paired risk-difference = 0.0, McNemar two-sided p = 1.0, 95% bootstrap CI = [0.0, 0.0] (10,000 resamples, seed 1729). Observing 0/300 violations gives a one-sided Clopper–Pearson 95% upper bound ≈ 0.00994 on an undetected baseline violation rate. Because the repair path was not exercised, this study quantifies that inserting a verifier does not change observed compliance when baseline generation already satisfies the safety predicate under the chosen contract; it does not provide evidence that verifier-guided repair can rescue genuine violations. We archive the preregistration, deterministic execution accounting, per-episode validator traces, and analysis artifacts to support reproducibility and to guide follow-up stress tests designed to exercise the repair path.

sections.introduction:
Automating intent-driven network configuration with large language models (LLMs) promises to speed operations but raises acute security concerns: an incorrectly synthesized configuration can expand attack surface, violate access-control policies, or break availability constraints. Prior systems and surveys therefore recommend constrained generation, execution oracles, and iterative generate–verify–repair (GVR) loops as operational mitigations. Yet there is limited preregistered, deterministic evidence specifically assessing whether embedding a verifier in a GVR loop reduces occurrences of security-relevant forbidden reachability under adversarially crafted intents.

We designed, preregistered, and executed a confirmatory paired experiment to answer the focused question: does embedding a reachability/policy verifier inside a GVR loop reduce the incidence of forbidden-reachability misconfigurations produced by an LLM-driven intent→configuration pipeline? The experiment fixes the model (declared gpt-5-mini), the execution contract (paired design with shared_initial_candidate semantics), and a deterministic validator set (two deterministic validators combined with logical OR), and it archives the complete deterministic artifacts (preregistration, execution manifest, per-episode validator traces, raw responses, and analysis outputs). The observed outcome was degenerate: every sampled intent produced configurations that satisfied the forbidden-reachability predicate in both arms (n11 = 300). This paper reports the preregistered design, deterministic execution, quantitative outcomes, statistical interpretation given the degenerate contingency, and artifact-grounded operational recommendations for follow-up stress tests meant to exercise verifier-triggered repair.
sections.related_work:
Our design and interpretation draw on three intersecting strands of verified literature. First, work on verifier-guided repair and execution-guided generation shows that feedback from oracles or runtime execution can substantially improve correctness for code and Infrastructure-as-Code tasks when the verifier has appropriate sensitivity and the repair policy is effective. Representative system papers, including TerraFormer (Jana et al.) and other recent GVR-style repair architectures, document scenarios in which verifier feedback materially reduces semantic errors on benchmarks, but observed gains depend strongly on verifier power and repair strategies.

Second, surveys and NetOps-focused system work document LLM failure modes—hallucination, overconfidence, and domain mismatch—and repeatedly recommend using validators, constrained generation, or human oversight to mitigate operational risk. Recent NetOps surveys and intent-to-configuration studies synthesize these operational risks and emphasize the need for execution-validated benchmarks and testbeds to evaluate safety interventions under controlled conditions.

Third, emulation/testbed and benchmarking work establishes that execution-based validation is feasible for research-grade evaluation (containerized FRRouting images, Mininet-style topologies, Batfish-like oracles, and lightweight static analyzers), but these papers also warn of external-validity gaps when porting results to heterogeneous production devices and live traffic. Existing literature rarely combines a preregistered paired evaluation, deterministic validators, and archived per-episode verifier traces focused specifically on security-relevant reachability predicates. Our study fills that procedural niche and intentionally reports a reproducible degenerate outcome to inform method design choices for future stress tests.
sections.methodology:
Design and estimand: The preregistration specified a paired binary design with N = 300 matched intents (150 benign seeds and 150 programmatic adversarial variants). The primary estimand is the paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline (absolute difference in the proportion of intents yielding forbidden reachability). The prespecified confirmatory test is an exact McNemar two-sided test (α = 0.05); paired bootstrap-percentile 95% confidence intervals were planned. Sensitivity checks treating technical failures as violations were prespecified; no technical failures occurred.

Generation contract and adapter semantics: To control hosted-model budget we used shared_initial_candidate semantics: for each pair a single LLM initial candidate was generated and replayed into both arms. This contract yields exactly one hosted-model call per pair (model_calls_used = 300 for 300 pairs) instead of two independent draws per pair (up to 600 calls). The design choice trades hosted-model cost for reduced between-arm sampling variability: because both arms evaluate the same initial candidate, the probability of producing discordant violating outputs across the pair is reduced. This trade-off is central to interpreting paired-test sensitivity for repair efficacy: repair can only act when the verifier detects a violation on the shared candidate.

Intervention and repair policy: Baseline is replay of the shared initial candidate. Guarded is the same shared candidate validated by two deterministic validators (a containerized execution-style reachability validator and a lightweight static reachability analyzer) combined with logical-OR: a pair is labeled violating if any validator reports forbidden reachability. The preregistered repair policy allowed up to one repair LLM call per pair and only when a validator-detected forbidden reachability occurred. Repair prompts and repair-call content were preregistered; no repair calls were triggered in the run because validators never reported violations.

Determinism, validators, and scoring: All emulator images, container seeds, orchestration parameters, and sampling seeds were fixed to ensure deterministic replay. Validators were deterministic by construction and their per-episode judgments (validation_before, validation_after, violation codes, repair_applied flags) were archived. The logical-OR scoring rule treats either validator reporting forbidden reachability as a violation, increasing sensitivity at the expense of possibly more false-positive detections if individual validators were overconservative.

Statistical interpretation plan: The planned paired test (McNemar) assesses whether the guarded arm reduces violations relative to baseline by comparing discordant pair counts (n10: guarded-only pass; n01: baseline-only pass). When discordant counts are zero the McNemar statistic is uninformative about repair efficacy. We therefore report the exact paired contingency, the McNemar p-value, and a descriptive Clopper–Pearson one-sided upper bound on the baseline violation probability conditional on observing zero violations across N independent episodes. We conducted the prespecified bootstrap CIs for the paired risk-difference with 10,000 resamples (bootstrap_seed = 1729) to reduce Monte Carlo error; the preregistration planned 1,000 resamples but the analysis used 10,000 (this analytic choice is archived and disclosed).
sections.results:
Execution and accounting: The run completed planned episodes = 600 (300 pairs × 2 conditions) with completed = 600 and failed episodes = 0. Under shared_initial_candidate semantics provider-call accounting recorded model_calls_used = 300. Deterministic reconciliation checks passed and provider-call audit shows 300 completed hosted-model call events with no cache hits.

Primary confirmatory outcome: Every paired intent satisfied the forbidden-reachability predicate in both arms. Aggregated counts: complete_pairs = 300, baseline_success_count = 300, guarded_success_count = 300. The paired contingency table is n11 = 300, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0 (Table 1). The paired risk-difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.0; exact McNemar two-sided p = 1.0. The prespecified paired bootstrap-percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples, seed 1729) is [0.0, 0.0].

Degenerate contingency and bounds: The absence of discordant pairs renders McNemar-style inference uninformative for assessing repair efficacy because there are no candidate cases where repair could have altered the binary outcome. As a descriptive constraint, observing 0 violations in N = 300 independent episodes yields a one-sided Clopper–Pearson 95% upper bound on the baseline violation probability of 1 − 0.05^(1/300) ≈ 0.00994 (≈0.994%). This bound quantifies the maximum baseline violation rate consistent with the observed zero-event outcome under an independent Bernoulli model; it does not provide evidence about repair ability.

Repair activity and validator concordance: Validators never reported forbidden reachability on any initial candidate; consequently no repair calls were invoked and all per-episode repair_applied flags are false. The two deterministic validators were concordant on all archived episodes. Representative per-episode validator traces, normalized configurations, difficulty annotations, and validation_before/after states are archived to enable inspection of typical tasks and validator judgments.
sections.discussion:
Interpretation of the degenerate outcome: Under the exact experimental contract (shared_initial_candidate), the declared model (gpt-5-mini), the evaluated deterministic validators combined by logical OR, and the sampled intents (150 benign + 150 programmatic adversarial variants), every generated shared candidate satisfied the forbidden-reachability predicate. Therefore, inserting the verifier in this configuration produced no observable change in compliance. This is a substantive, artifact-grounded finding about the joint system under these fixed choices—not evidence that verifiers are unnecessary in general.

Why the repair path was not exercised: Two coupled design facts explain the absence of repair opportunities. First, shared_initial_candidate semantics collapses cross-condition sampling variance because both arms evaluate the same candidate; discordance that could reveal repair potential is thereby less likely. Second, the deterministic adversarial perturbations used here did not produce validator-detectable forbidden reachability for the chosen model and validators. Either factor alone could reduce the number of cases where repair would be triggered; together they produced the degenerate contingency.

Operational implications and design recommendations: (1) For experiments intended to evaluate repair efficacy, prefer independent-condition generation (two independent LLM draws per pair) or increase the repair-call budget so that repair can be attempted on additional candidates; both increase the probability of producing discordant outcomes and exercising repair. (2) Adversary potency must be calibrated to the verifier's sensitivity: programmatic adversarial variants should be targeted to violate the concrete predicates the validators detect; otherwise the repair pathway remains untested. (3) Verifier diversity and strength matter: combining multiple, stronger execution oracles (including production-grade device emulators or richer policy-checking engines) can expose different failure modes. (4) Budget–determinism trade-offs must be explicit: shared_initial_candidate semantics provides deterministic, low-cost accounting but reduces the chance to observe repair opportunities; experimenters must choose the contract appropriate to their estimand.

Methodological note on inference under degenerate results: When paired discordant counts are zero, exact paired tests cannot estimate a paired reduction in violations because no repair opportunities were observed. Reporting the exact contingency, the McNemar p-value, and a one-sided Clopper–Pearson upper bound on the baseline violation probability transparently communicates what the data constrain and what remains unresolved. This pattern of reporting preserves confirmatory integrity while guiding follow-up stress experiments.

Threats to validity and scope: Internal validity is limited by the shared_initial_candidate semantics and single-model scope. Construct validity depends on whether the forbidden-reachability predicate and the two deterministic validators adequately represent operational security risk. External validity is constrained because tasks were synthetic and executed in deterministic FRRouting-style emulation; results may not generalize to production devices, live traffic, or different operational constraints. Conclusion validity is constrained because the observed contingency violates power assumptions used in the preregistration. These limitations motivate targeted follow-up tests rather than reinterpretation of the present confirmatory outcome.
sections.conclusion: We executed a preregistered paired evaluation of a verifier-in-the-loop GVR pipeline for intent→configuration generation with a declared LLM (gpt-5-mini), two deterministic validators combined by logical OR, and a shared_initial_candidate generation contract. The run completed N = 300 matched pairs with model_calls_used = 300 and produced a degenerate outcome: both baseline and guarded arms passed the forbidden-reachability predicate on all pairs (n11 = 300). Because validators never reported violations, the repair path was not exercised and the experiment cannot assess whether verifier-guided repair rescues violating outputs. The result is evidence-grounded: inserting a verifier under these precise contract choices did not change observed compliance because baseline generation already satisfied the safety predicate. Design choices—generation semantics (shared vs independent draws), adversary design, repair budget, verifier strength, and model diversity—materially determine whether a verifier-in-the-loop architecture can be shown to reduce security-relevant misconfigurations. We release the preregistration, execution manifest, per-episode validator traces, raw responses, and analysis artifacts in an archived evidence bundle to enable reproducibility and to inform follow-up stress tests that intentionally exercise repair paths.

limitations: Degenerate confirmatory outcome: zero discordant pairs (n11 = 300, n10 = n01 = n00 = 0) render McNemar inference uninformative about repair efficacy when baseline violation rates are nonzero; the preregistered power calculation assumed a nonzero baseline violation rate and targeted detecting a 30 percentage-point absolute reduction.

GVR not exercised: under the chosen task set, emulator, model, and validators the verifier never reported forbidden reachability and consequently the guarded repair step was never invoked; the experiment therefore tests whether verifier insertion changes compliance when baseline is already compliant, not whether verifier-guided repair rescues violations.

Generation contract choice: the preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics produced one LLM call per pair and reduced model-call overhead but also limited independent draws that could produce discordant errors; alternative contracts (independent-condition generation or expanded repair budgets) would better exercise repair paths.

Adversarial-perturbation detail: the preregistration specified programmatic generation of one adversarial variant per benign seed; per-task generation seeds and intent payloads are archived in the evidence bundle for reproducibility.

External validity: tasks were synthetically generated and executed in deterministic FRRouting-style emulation; results do not necessarily generalize to heterogeneous production devices, live traffic conditions, or different operational constraints.
Model and verifier scope: a single model (gpt-5-mini) and two deterministic validators were evaluated; other LLMs, stronger verifiers, or dynamic execution oracles may produce different outcomes.
